faqs.a: Bcrypt is a password-hashing function designed in 1999 for securely storing passwords. Unlike fast hashes such as MD5 or SHA-256, bcrypt is intentionally slow and includes a built-in salt and an adjustable cost factor, which makes brute-force and rainbow-table attacks impractical.

The cost factor controls how much work bcrypt does: the number of iterations equals 2 raised to the cost. Cost 10 means 1024 iterations, cost 12 means 4096, and so on. Each increment roughly doubles hashing time, so higher costs are stronger against attackers but slower for legitimate logins. Cost 10–12 is the common range today.
faqs.q: What does the cost factor (rounds) mean?

faqs.a: Because a fresh random 22-character salt is generated every time. The salt is stored inside the hash itself, so verification can re-derive it. Different-looking hashes of the same password all verify correctly — this is a security feature, not a bug.
faqs.q: Why do two hashes of the same password look different?

faqs.a: The algorithm is real bcrypt, so the output is cryptographically identical to server-side hashes. This page runs entirely offline in your browser with no network calls. Still, treat it as a development utility: in production, hash passwords on your own trusted server, and never paste real user passwords into any web page.
faqs.q: Is hashing a password in the browser safe?

faqs.a: Bcrypt only processes the first 72 bytes of input; anything beyond that is silently ignored. This is a quirk of the original algorithm. If your users type passphrases longer than that, consider pre-hashing with SHA-256 before bcrypt, a pattern many frameworks use.
faqs.q: What is the maximum password length?

faqs.a: It is the bcrypt version identifier. $2a$ was the original, $2b$ fixed a minor wrapping bug in some implementations, and $2y$ is used by crypt_blowfish to mark correct handling. All three verify the same way; $2b$ is the modern default you will see most often.
faqs.q: What does $2b$ mean in the hash?

bcrypt-hash-generator.formula:
hash = bcrypt(password, random_salt, cost)

Hash format:  $2b$ + cost (2 digits) + $ + 22-char salt + 31-char hash
Iterations = 2 ^ cost   (cost 10 means 1024 key-expansion rounds)
howTo: Type the password you want to hash into the password field. Nothing is sent anywhere; it stays in your browser.
Choose the cost factor with the slider. 10 is the common default; higher numbers are stronger but slower.
Click Generate hash and wait a moment — real bcrypt work is intentionally slow.
Copy the resulting 60-character hash with the copy button, or download it as a text file.
To verify, paste an existing hash and type the candidate password in the verify section, then click Verify.
keyFacts: Bcrypt was designed by Niels Provos and David Mazieres in 1999 specifically for password storage, based on the Blowfish cipher.
Every hash is 60 characters long and carries its own version, cost factor, and 22-character salt, so no separate salt column is needed.
The cost factor (rounds) is adaptive: raising it by 1 roughly doubles hashing time, letting hashes stay strong as hardware gets faster.
A fresh random salt is generated for every hash, so hashing the same password twice produces two completely different strings.
Bcrypt is one-way: a hash cannot be reversed back into the password. Verification works by hashing the candidate password with the stored salt and comparing.
Bcrypt truncates passwords at 72 bytes, so extremely long passphrases get silently cut — a known quirk every developer should be aware of.

bcrypt-hash-generator.workedExample:
Password: MySecret123, cost factor: 10.
Generated hash: $2b$10$G5cGqYjlwu/rWdwlEu6fFuVUPERhY6fRq1qmoc/yvyDCsN9CAZkni
Reading it: $2b$ is the version, 10 is the cost (2^10 = 1024 iterations), and the remaining 53 characters are the salt plus the hash. Run the same input again and the salt — hence the whole string — will be different, yet both hashes will verify against the same password.
